title: Francis kisses the leper
hookLine: the rich young man who feared lepers dismounts and kisses one
last: THE LONG WAY IS THE WAY.

lines: A RICH YOUNG MAN ON A HORSE.
cards: A young man is riding on the plain below Assisi. He's the son of a cloth merchant, used to money, fine clothes and good company. And there's one sight he can't bear: people with leprosy.
By his own later account, even seeing them was bitter to him. Now, on the road ahead, there's a man with leprosy. Everything in the rider wants to look away and ride on.
Instead, his early biographers say, he gets down from his horse. He gives the man money. And he kisses his hand.

teach.b: The young man is Francis of Assisi. Near the end of his life, in the short text called his Testament, he looked back on this as where his new life began.
In paraphrase: when I was in sin, it seemed too bitter to me to see lepers.

teach.h: THE LORD HIMSELF LED ME AMONG THEM.
teach.b: And the Lord himself led me among them, and I showed mercy to them.
And when I left them, what had seemed bitter to me was turned into sweetness of soul and body. Notice who leads in his telling. Not Francis: the Lord himself led me among them.
And notice what changed. Not the people with leprosy; they were exactly who they had been. What changed was what tasted bitter and what tasted sweet, inside Francis.
His biographers add that soon afterward he went to live among them, washing their sores and serving them, kissing hands he once couldn't look at.

In Matthew's Gospel, a man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Matthew writes, in the King James words: "Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him, saying, I will; be thou clean." He touched him.
Before anything else happened, a hand reached out. Francis's kiss on the road echoes that reach. One word about words.
The old word leper names a person by an illness. This lesson says people with leprosy where it can. The title keeps the old word because the old stories use it.

how: Franciscan friars and sisters, and other Christians inspired by Francis, often serve people who are sick, poor or shunned, and Franciscans still read his Testament as a key to how his life changed.

the sight of lepers, at first

s: Francis was at ease with people with leprosy from the start
by his own account, even seeing them was bitter to him, until he was led among them.
in Matthew, Jesus touches the man with leprosy
"Jesus put forth his hand, and touched him."
in his Testament, Francis says he changed all by himself

games.q: you're Francis, riding near Assisi. a man with leprosy is on the road ahead, and you can't bear the sight. what do you do?
o: get down, give him money and kiss his hand.
games.why: his early biographers say he dismounted, gave the man money and kissed his hand. in his own telling, what had been bitter turned sweet.

practice: Bring to mind one thing or one person you steer around: a neighbor, a phone call, a part of town, a conversation.
Without forcing anything, picture yourself getting down from the horse, stopping, then stepping a little closer, and notice what happens in you as you come nearer.
If you pray, ask to be led, the way Francis said he was; if you don't, stay near it in your mind, breathing, without riding off.

wordCard.voice: Leprosy. The illness that young Francis of Assisi feared, until he got down from his horse and kissed the hand of a man who had it, and what was bitter turned sweet.

carryVoice: Your line: what was bitter became sweet. In his telling, the Lord did the leading. See you tomorrow.
